articles.title: [Perspectives] John Wong: making an impact on population health at scale
articles.abstract: “I’m concerned that the narrative now around ageing populations is one of doom and gloom. But long-lived populations are not the problem. The problem is that we haven’t allowed people to get to an older age healthy”, says John Wong, Executive Director of the Centre for Population Health at the National University of Singapore (NUS) and Executive Director of The Yong Pung How and Yong Wei-Woo Centre at the National University Health System (NUHS), Singapore. “Two-thirds of the world is now below the fertility replacement rate, and unless we keep our populations healthy throughout their whole lifespan, we’ll have this major challenge of more and more unwell older people”, continued Wong, who is also Isabel Chan Professor in Medical Sciences in the Division of Haematology-Oncology at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, NUS, and Emeritus Consultant in the Department of Haematology-Oncology, National University Cancer Institute, NUHS, Singapore.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Shadows and interiority
articles.abstract: American television series The Pitt may have redefined the popularity of medical drama, but hospitals have always provided a rich seam for creatives, whether their medium is page or screen. From novels like Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's 1966 Soviet-era Cancer Ward and Abraham Verghese's epic saga Cutting for Stone (2009) all the way through to television dramas such as Casualty, ER, and Grey's Anatomy, it seems we can’t get enough of human stories played out in a tense clinical setting. This is the absolute opposite of what author Chloe Aridjis does in The Shadow of the Object.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Temporal rationing: a man with gastric cancer in Colombia
articles.abstract: Pepe, a 45-year-old man living in the city of Cali, Colombia, worked as a self-employed hauler of goods with a wheelbarrow. In 2010, he presented to a general practitioner with several months of abdominal heaviness and non-exertional substernal burning. The physician provisionally diagnosed gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and prescribed omeprazole. However, Pepe's symptoms slowly worsened and 10 weeks later he returned to the physician, who ordered a gastroscopy, which occurred 2 months later, revealing an ulcerated mass.

articles.title: [Correspondence] WHO should adjust its cervical cancer plan
articles.abstract: In Gary M Clifford's Comment, he observed that the dominant driver of global inequalities in cervical cancer burden, which are poised to increase dramatically, is unequal access to cervical screening.1 WHO perpetuates such inequalities by offering paradoxical guidance for low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where 95% of global cervical cancer deaths occur.2 In 2000, the WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer's (IARC) Head of Cancer Screening stated he would be “loath to recommend starting a screening programme with conventional Paps in a country with no current screening programme in place”.

articles.title: [Correspondence] WHO should adjust its cervical cancer plan – Authors’ reply
articles.abstract: We agree with Eric J Suba that current global inequalities in cervical cancer burden are driven largely by unequal access to effective screening programmes. This point was highlighted by Brisson and colleagues1 and in an accompanying Comment2 that warned that human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination implementation must not follow the same inequitable path.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Optimising standard of care in non-small-cell lung cancer trials
articles.abstract: We read Anwen Xiong and colleagues’ study with great interest.1 Despite the established first-line role of immune checkpoint inhibitors in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without targetable genomic alterations, outcomes remain poor. In the phase 3 OptiTROP-Lung05 trial, sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT) plus pembrolizumab showed a significant improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) compared with pembrolizumab monotherapy (median not reached vs 5·7 months; hazard ratio 0·35, 95% CI 0·26–0·47) in programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1)-positive advanced NSCLC (PD-L1 tumour proportion score ≥1%).

articles.title: [Correspondence] Optimising standard of care in non-small-cell lung cancer trials – Authors’ reply
articles.abstract: We thank Emma D A Wagener and Wouter H van Geffen for emphasising the importance of comparator selection. We agree that pembrolizumab plus platinum-based chemotherapy is commonly preferred for many patients with a programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumour proportion score (TPS) of 1–49%, and that OptiTROP-Lung05 was not designed to establish superiority of sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab over chemoimmunotherapy.1

articles.title: FDA Approves New Treatment for Advanced Pancreatic Cancer
articles.abstract: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a first-in-class therapy for patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer.

articles.title: Error in Results
articles.abstract: The Original Investigation titled “Adjuvant Nivolumab vs Observation in Resected Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” published on June 1, 2026, was corrected to fix typographical errors in the text, including indicating that the trial was stopped for futility at 75% information, rather than 78%, and the number of participants lost to follow-up in the nivolumab group in Figure 1. This article was corrected online.

articles.title: From Biological Insight to a New Class of Medicines for Hemophilia A
articles.abstract: The 2026 Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award winners describe the development of a bispecific antibody that mimics blood coagulation factor VIII, revolutionizing the treatment of hemophilia, a life-threatening bleeding disorder caused by lack of factor VIII.

articles.title: Tucidinostat Plus R-CHOP for Large B-Cell Lymphoma
articles.abstract: To the Editor Dr Xu and colleagues conducted an important randomized study evaluating the efficacy and safety of tucidinostat added to standard rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) compared with R-CHOP alone as first-line therapy for patients with MYC/BCL2 double-expressor diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. A total of 423 patients were randomized to receive oral tucidinostat or matching placebo in combination with 6 cycles of R-CHOP. The primary end point was event-free survival. The stratified hazard ratio for event-free survival was 0.72 (95% CI, 0.54-0.96; P = .02), favoring the tucidinostat group. However, no statistically significant differences were observed for any secondary end point.

articles.title: Tucidinostat Plus R-CHOP for Large B-Cell Lymphoma—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Ms Armbruster and colleagues for their thoughtful comments on our randomized clinical trial evaluating tucidinostat plus R-CHOP vs R-CHOP alone in patients with MYC/BCL2 double-expressor diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. We appreciate their reanalysis using restricted mean survival time, which provides a clinically intuitive measure of treatment effect and can be useful as a complementary approach, in cases in which the proportional hazards assumption is questionable.

articles.title: [Editorial] Microplastics and cancer: a looming threat?
articles.abstract: Microplastics are a growing global concern and have been linked to various health conditions. A study presented by Ilias Dimeas and colleagues at the 2026 European Respiratory Society conference found a higher burden of microplastics in the lungs of patients with lung cancer than in those without cancer. In the study, 70% of 100 people undergoing a bronchoscopy had detectable microplastics in at least one sample, and patients with lung cancer were more likely to have detectable microplastics in their samples than patients without lung cancer.

articles.title: [Comment] Exercise oncology: from trials and guidelines to routine clinical care
articles.abstract: In oncology practice, there are trade-offs between quality of life and survival for many therapies. Similar trade-offs exist for drug reimbursement based on therapeutic effectiveness, affected population, and cost.

articles.title: [Comment] Looking at cancer burden in Africa through a new lens
articles.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of death and disability globally, with a disproportionate rising burden in Africa.1,2 Effective policy response has been consistently hampered by fragmented and incomplete cancer surveillance data.3 For a long time, there has been an assumption that a global uniform framework for understanding cancer risk factors exists and is applicable universally.4 This concept of harmonised global data is plausible in well structured and well resourced health systems in which research and care systems are integrated—systems that exist mostly in high-income regions.

articles.title: [Comment] Personalised medicine in oncology: inequality aversion in a fast-moving field
articles.abstract: Personalised medicine has been shown to improve patient care and holds promise to further benefit treatment results. The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research provides an overview of state-of-the-art treatments and the situation in low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs). From targeted treatment using companion diagnostics, identifying targets to guide treatment decisions, to broad ‘omics testing in cancer of unknown primary and metastasised tumours, the field is vast and inequalities exist within and between countries.

articles.title: [Comment] Ethical priorities in global cancer genomics and precision oncology
articles.abstract: Amid the promise of cancer genomics and precision oncology lies complex and ethically weighty issues. Genomics and other ‘omics are undoubtedly transforming cancer care for thousands of patients annually, enabling better prognosis, access to treatments or trials, or informing relatives. Yet, these interventions overwhelmingly benefit people in high-income countries: they are failing to reach most patients with cancer who could benefit, and those who are reached could, for reasons including health system readiness or data representation and interpretation, receive no or marginal benefit to their care.

articles.title: [Comment] Inequities in access to precision oncology: shared challenges, unified blueprint
articles.abstract: Precision oncology has substantially changed the therapeutic landscape from a “one size fits all” approach to that of individualised (or personalised) treatments.1 The promise of precision oncology extends across the entire cancer continuum from prevention, early diagnosis, subtyping of tumours, treatment selection, risk-adapted therapies, development of novel anticancer medicines, and post-treatment surveillance.2 The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research focuses on the current challenges and practical solutions to faciliate wider implementation.

articles.title: [Comment] Beyond the evidence: why multistakeholder cooperation will determine whether cancer genomics reaches patients
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology presents a worrying picture.1 While the number of precision oncology drugs continues to increase,2,3 access to testing and matched therapies remains profoundly unequal, research is concentrated in high-income countries (HICs) and populations of European ancestry, and expanding testing capacity has not always translated into proportionate population-level benefit. The Commission's survey of national cancer control programmes (NCCPs), conducted in collaboration with the Union for International Cancer Control and WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) across 34 countries, found partial integration of genomics into most NCCPs, including in HICs.

articles.title: [Comment] Ecological neglect: critical oversight in precision oncology governance
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research1 examines the gap between the promise of precision oncology and its delivery across global health systems. Raffaella Casolino and colleagues argue that precision oncology has advanced with remarkable speed, yet its clinical impact and sustainability remain uneven, meaning that for much of the world, precision oncology remains just a promise. The authors argue that if the vision of precision oncology is to be realised, health systems need to generate, integrate, govern, and learn from data.

articles.title: [Comment] Affordability in the era of precision oncology
articles.abstract: Cancer drugs are increasingly unaffordable for health systems. Global spending on cancer drugs will reach US$441 billion by 2029.1 This 75% increase over 5 years cannot be explained by population ageing or changing prevalence alone. Instead, the price of cancer drugs is driving accelerated spending growth.2 Rising prices place considerable pressure on health systems, particularly when increased spending is not matched by commensurate improvements in patient health. Unfortunately, many expensive cancer drugs have highly uncertain safety and efficacy evidence at the time of market authorisation.

articles.title: [Comment] Counting who was not tested: artificial intelligence extraction of genomic and treatment data from hospital records
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable access to cancer genomics and precision oncology provides an important framework defining indicators that health systems can and should measure.1 Operationalising these indicators, however, requires substantial data infrastructure. One indicator in the Commission's Precision Oncology Access Cascade defines the group of eligible patients who receive recommended genomic testing. The number of patients tested is relatively straightforward to obtain; however, the number meeting the guideline criteria is not because this information is usually recorded as unstructured narrative text rather than as a structured field.

articles.title: [Comment] Blank spaces on the map: genomics for global cancer research
articles.abstract: For most of the history of cancer genomics, the map of our knowledge has had blank spaces on it. In the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes, for example, roughly three quarters of donors were of European descent; samples from Latin American donors made up only about 1% of the large public repositories and samples from patients of Middle Eastern descent were almost entirely absent.1

articles.title: [Comment] England's National Cancer Plan; ambition without accountability
articles.abstract: Publication of England's National Cancer Control Plan (NCCP) in February, 2026,1 marked a hard-won achievement, after years of advocacy from patients, clinicians, charities, parliamentarians, and The Lancet Oncology.2,3 The expectation was to address long-standing systemic issues in treatment delays and quality, workforce shortages, and inequalities; but hopes were quickly dashed.4 The plan had no real new money, no additional workforce capacity, no expansion of treatment infrastructure, no prioritisation, and no implementation strategy.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Re-evaluating aglatimagene in localised prostate cancer
articles.abstract: We read with great interest the Article by Theodore L DeWeese and colleagues detailing the results of the PrTK03 phase 3 trial, which evaluated the addition of aglatimagene besadenovec (CAN-2409) and valacyclovir to standard-of-care external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) for localised prostate cancer.1 We commend the investigators for executing this decade-spanning study. The biological premise—using an adenoviral vector to exert localised cytotoxicity of a systemically administered prodrug while stimulating a T-cell-mediated immune response—is scientifically sound.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Re-evaluating aglatimagene in localised prostate cancer – Authors' reply
articles.abstract: We thank Thomas Büttner and colleagues for their interest in our Article on the PrTK03 trial.1 In our trial, disease-free survival was the prospectively specified, US Food and Drug Administration-agreed primary endpoint under a Special Protocol Assessment, analysed in the intention-to-treat population and defined to include local failure, including positive biopsy, regional failure, distant metastasis, or death.1 The US Food and Drug Administration did not agree to use biochemical failure as a disease-free survival event.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Proton pump inhibitors and durvalumab in PACIFIC
articles.abstract: Leonardo Brunetti and colleagues’ post-hoc analysis of the PACIFIC trial in The Lancet Oncology addresses an important and clinically timely question: whether baseline exposure to proton pump inhibitors or antibiotics modifies the benefit of durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy in patients with unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer.1 The observed association between proton pump inhibitor exposure and inferior progression-free and overall survival in the durvalumab group, but not in the placebo group, is thought provoking.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Proton pump inhibitors and durvalumab in PACIFIC – Authors' reply
articles.abstract: We thank our colleagues for their thoughtful comments on our post-hoc analysis of PACIFIC.1 Their correspondence raises two issues: the definition of survival events and whether proton pump inhibitor exposure is causal or reflects its prescribing context.

articles.title: [News] Trump cuts childhood vaccine recommendations
articles.abstract: The US President Donald Trump has issued an executive order stressing “maximal parental choice” and cutting the number of childhood vaccines recommended by the federal government to 11 from 18.

articles.title: [News] Nigeria plans major expansion of radiotherapy capacity
articles.abstract: Africa's most populous country Nigeria plans to procure and install 35 additional linear accelerators (LINACs), substantially expanding its radiotherapy capacity. Six Cancer Centres of Excellence are also being developed, with centres in Katsina, Enugu, and Benin completed and commissioned. However, the new machines translating into wider access depends on availability of specialist staffing, maintenance, financing, and where the additional capacity is located.

articles.title: [News] Delays in cancer referrals and care lead to harm and missed diagnoses in England
articles.abstract: Late and missed diagnoses, delays in cancer care, and physical harm were partly caused by England's National Health Service (NHS) system for general practitioners (GPs) seeking specialist advice before patient referral to hospital, according to an investigation by the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB).

articles.title: [News] Increased tobacco production and cigarette imports in Africa
articles.abstract: While tobacco-leaf production across the world declined by 19% between 2012 and 2024, it increased by 9% in Africa, according to a WHO analysis published on Aug 31, 2026. Moreover, during this period, there was a more than two-times increase in cigarette imports to Africa—from US$833 million to $1·77 billion.

articles.title: [News] 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer
articles.abstract: Interim results from the phase 3 ARTEMIS-008 trial, presented by Jie Wang (Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, China), suggest risvutatug rezetecan, a B7-H3-directed antibody–drug conjugate (ADC), could be the new standard of care in relapsed small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive risvutatug rezetecan (8·0 mg/kg; n=230) or topotecan (1·2 mg/m2 on days 1–5; n=231) every 3 weeks. At a median follow-up of 12·2 months, overall survival (the primary endpoint) was significantly improved with risvutatug rezetecan compared with topotecan (18·5 vs 10·3 months; HR 0·46 [95% CI 0·35–0·62).

articles.title: [News] Kenya agrees major cuts to cancer drug prices
articles.abstract: The Kenyan Government has agreed a deal with Pfizer that could reduce the price of selected cancer medicines by seven times. Costs are expected to drop from as much as 1 million Kenyan Shillings (KSh; US$7725) to below KSh50 000 ($386) per treatment cycle for some drugs. The agreement covers nine cancers: breast, stomach, colorectal, lung, prostate, and oesophageal cancers, as well as leukaemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma.

articles.title: [News] Toxic dust around the World Trade Center
articles.abstract: On Sept 8, 2026, New York City authorities released more than 170 000 pages of documents showing that officials misled the public about toxic air quality levels after the Sept 11, 2001, attack that killed more than 2600 people at the World Trade Center (WTC). Health researchers say the documents contain little medical information that is new but confirm that carcinogens and toxins were present months after the attacks, exposing 400 000 people in lower Manhattan to smoke, dust, and combustion products.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Cancer's new anxiety: not a death sentence, but delay
articles.abstract: Throughout the history of cancer research, hyperbole has never been in short supply—whether it be Richard Nixon's war, Joe Biden's moonshot, or Cancer Research UK's 2023 declaration of a golden era. Driving such rhetoric has been the need to act against an enduring societal concern—cancer, the so-called Big C, society's number one fear.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Against cancer, not against dying: Ernest Becker in the oncology clinic
articles.abstract: When American cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker was awarded the 1974 Pulitzer Prize for his book, The Denial of Death, he had died of colorectal cancer only 2 months earlier. More than half a century later, the book feels almost uncomfortably contemporary in the oncology clinic. Although the book does not address cancer care directly, it speaks to what cancer reveals: mortality, and the symbolic structures we build to make that knowledge bearable. For Becker, identities, professions, institutions, religions, families, reputations, and achievements are ways in which the fragile self seeks continuity beyond finitude.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Sir Chris Hoy's Tour de 4 charity cycle ride returns
articles.abstract: Mention the name Chris Hoy and it's natural to picture the Olympic cyclist, who won six gold medals and one silver in Sydney, Athens, Beijing, and London between 2000 and 2012. Fans voted for him to be named as the BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2008, and he was knighted by the late Queen Elizabeth in the 2009 New Year honours list. However, over the past 2 years, Hoy has become famous for a completely different reason. In October, 2024, he revealed that he had received a terminal diagnosis of stage-4 prostate cancer, which had spread to his bones.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Differing approaches to cancer at the Edinburgh Fringe
articles.abstract: “I had cancer a couple of years ago—I don’t like to talk about it,” grinned comedian Matt Forde during his show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the world's largest arts festival, which took place in Edinburgh, UK, on Aug 7–31, 2026. With a sly grin at his audience, he added “I’m not going to use it to sell tickets for another sold out night in Edinburgh.” Forde, who is best known for his impressions of politicians, was diagnosed in July, 2023, with a chordoma, a very rare sarcoma at the base of his spine.

articles.title: [Articles] Chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab followed by maintenance pembrolizumab with or without olaparib as first-line treatment of patients with advanced BRCA non-mutated epithelial ovarian cancer (ENGOT-OV43/GOG-3036/KEYLYNK-001): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy followed by maintenance with pembrolizumab–olaparib showed a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival versus chemotherapy, suggesting that this regimen might have potential for patients with newly diagnosed BRCA non-mutated stage III–IV epithelial ovarian cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] Global burden of cancer attributable to infections in 2024: a worldwide incidence analysis
articles.abstract: Our findings highlight the importance of infection control to achieve cancer prevention. Scientifically proven, but often underused, approaches include HPV and HBV vaccination; testing and treatment of HIV, H pylori, HBV, and HCV; safe injection practices; access to condoms and pre-exposure prophylaxis to prevent HIV transmission; and screening of precancerous lesions for HPV-driven cervical and anal cancer. Our findings also inform the investment cases for research and development for new prevention tools, most notably for EBV.

articles.title: [Articles] Hypofractionated versus conventional fractionated postmastectomy radiotherapy for patients with high-risk breast cancer (CHN HYPOPMRT): 10-year outcomes from a randomised, non-inferiority, open-label, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: Hypofractionated postmastectomy radiotherapy provided durable locoregional control with no increase in severe late adverse events compared with conventional fractionation, supporting its use as a more time-efficient option than conventional fractionated radiotherapy.

articles.title: [Articles] Patient-reported symptom monitoring in patients with lung cancer (SYMPRO-Lung trial): long-term, post-hoc survival results of a multicentre, stepped-wedged, cluster-randomised clinical trial
articles.abstract: Weekly PRO symptom monitoring was associated with meaningful improvement in long-term overall survival among patients with stage I–IV lung cancer. Median overall survival was 5 months longer in the intervention group than in the control group. These findings underscore the value of implementing PRO symptom monitoring within routine care for patients with lung cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] An integrated lifestyle intervention for mitigation of adverse effects associated with androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer (STAMINA): a multicentre, randomised trial
articles.abstract: The STAMINA lifestyle intervention meets best practice guidelines, can be implemented in NHS trusts in England, and offers clinicians a clear basis for identification and prescription of a supervised exercise and dietary advice intervention to mitigate negative effects associated with ADT.

articles.title: [Articles] Development and external validation of a new prognostic model for metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma: a preregistered analysis using data from randomised clinical trials in the checkpoint inhibitor era
articles.abstract: The CPI2 model, using 14 readily available clinical parameters, demonstrated improvement in discriminative accuracy compared with the IMDC model. This classification should be further validated in other trial and observational populations and be used to reanalyse heterogeneity of treatment effects of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination regimens in trials shaping the current and future treatment landscape.

articles.title: [Articles] Long-term exposure to wildfire-related PM2·5 and overall survival of older patients with lung cancer: a retrospective, registry-based cohort study
articles.abstract: Wildfire-related PM2·5 showed greater toxicity per unit exposure than non-wildfire PM2·5. As wildfire-related PM2·5 is the fastest-growing contributor to ambient air pollution, there is an urgent need for updated strategies to manage wildfires and mitigate their effects.

articles.title: [Articles] Burden of cancer in Africa, 1990–2023: a systematic analysis from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
articles.abstract: Cancer is a growing contributor to the disease burden in Africa, with rising cases, deaths, and DALYs disproportionately affecting children, adolescents, and young adults. The increase in age-standardised mortality and DALY rates stands in sharp contrast to the ambitions of the Sustainable Development Goals for 2030 and the African Union Agenda 2063. Addressing this burden will require coordinated national and international action, with health-system strengthening and context-specific cancer-control strategies spanning prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment.

articles.title: [The Lancet Oncology Commission] Accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research: a Lancet Oncology Commission
articles.abstract: Cancer genomics and precision oncology are increasingly central to cancer care, but many health systems struggle to implement them equitably, effectively, and sustainably. This Commission defines the current global precision oncology landscape and analyses the scientific, structural, and health-system challenges shaping its delivery and impact. Findings indicate that access to cancer genomics and precision oncology remains profoundly unequal across and within countries, leaving millions of patients without guideline-indicated interventions each year.

articles.title: [Clinical Picture] Not all thoracic micronodules are metastases
articles.abstract: A 58-year-old female, lifelong non-smoker with history of Parkinson's disease, presented with a palpable right breast lump to the Odette Cancer Centre at Sunnybrook Health and Sciences Centre (Toronto, ON, Canada) in April, 2024, and was diagnosed with right-sided oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2-positive breast cancer (cT3N0). She received neoadjuvant dose dense doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab. Lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed revealing a pathological complete response.

articles.title: Chronotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors: The knowns, the unknowns, and the contested
articles.abstract: Emerging data indicate that immune checkpoint inhibitors can exhibit time-of-day-dependent effects in pre-clinical models. Furthermore, multiple retrospective clinical trials associate earlier anti-tumor treatment timing with improved outcomes. However, key questions remain regarding the reproducibility of these findings, the underlying mechanisms, and their clinical implications. This commentary discusses these open questions and provides an outlook on the field.

articles.title: Human-centric preclinical models for CAR T cell therapy in solid tumors: Where patient-derived organoids fit
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has shown promising activity in solid tumors, yet translational progress remains limited by preclinical models that incompletely capture human tumor biology. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) preserve key features of human tumors, including cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture, thereby enabling functional evaluation of CAR T cell targets, next-generation approaches, resistance mechanisms, and selected safety considerations. We discuss how PDOs complement existing preclinical platforms to support CAR T cell development for solid tumors.

articles.title: γδ T cells BiTE back at small cell lung cancer
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Ng et al. characterize and leverage cytotoxic γδ T cells in small cell lung cancer to overcome unsuccessful checkpoint blockade immunotherapy. Engaging Vδ2+ cells with a bispecific T cell engager (BiTE) bypasses the challenge of low MHC-I expression and ineffective CD8+ T cells.

articles.title: Microbial cues for a stem-like lymphoid niche
articles.abstract: While tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) broadly correlate with immunotherapy efficacy, their functional heterogeneity can translate into divergent clinical outcomes. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hu et al. uncover a microbiota-orchestrated stem-like lymphoid niche in which CD70+ ILC2s sustain progenitor exhausted T cells, and their findings redefine the functional organization underlying TLS-associated antitumor immunity.

articles.title: Teamwork makes the dream work? Ensemble learning in computational pathology
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Luo et al. report an ensemble approach that integrates five pretrained pathology foundation models into a slide-level representation to exploit their complementary information, yielding improvements in tumor subtyping, biomarker, and therapy-response prediction. This shows the potential of ensemble and multimodal approaches in computational pathology.

articles.title: Hitting KRAS G12D without the gut punch: Can immunotherapy make it last?
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Shi et al. report encouraging early-phase results combining HRS-4642, an allele-specific KRAS G12D inhibitor, with the PD-L1 inhibitor adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer. The intravenous combination was safe and well tolerated, notably sparing patients the gastrointestinal toxicity common to oral KRAS inhibitors, and achieved a promising 43% response rate at the recommended dose.

articles.title: Beyond genes and hotspots: Protein-informed interpretation of cancer mutations
articles.abstract: Interpreting the biological and clinical significance of somatic mutations in cancer genomes remains challenging. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hyeon et al. identify and map significantly mutated regions to protein domains and structural features, establishing a proteo-genomics framework for interpreting cancer mutations beyond genes and hotspots.

articles.title: The wu wei of brain metastases: When the gift of a pause is also a vulnerability
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, García-Gómez et al. show that brain-seeding cancer cells exploit an MXD4-dependent proliferative pause that enables survival under stress before metastatic outgrowth. By restraining MYC and activating protective stress responses, this pause becomes an Achilles’ heel, potentially targetable to eradicate micrometastases before clinical relapse.

articles.title: Tumor cells recruit macrophage bodyguards to outlast chemotherapy
articles.abstract: In Cell Press Blue, Carvalho et al. identify spatially organized tumor-macrophage niches, EMT-like CD44high cancer cells paired with SPP1/PARP14high macrophages, that drive chemoresistance in bladder cancer. PARP14 inhibition can flip this protective niche into an inflammatory, cisplatin-sensitizing state.

articles.title: Beyond BMI: The diet-microbiome context of the obesity paradox
articles.abstract: In Nature, Desharnais et al. show that in diverse mouse models, anti-PD-1 sensitivity is more closely linked to diet-microbiome-metabolite ecosystem than to obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction. Their findings reinforce body mass index (BMI) as an incomplete proxy for host biology and suggest strategies to improve anti-PD-1 efficacy without inducing obesity.

articles.title: γδ T cells modulate anti-tumor immunity in small cell lung cancer
articles.abstract: Ng et al. show that γδ T cells infiltrate SCLC and have cancer-fighting abilities. These cells can be harnessed through multiple therapeutics to kill SCLC, including through MHC-independent recognition mechanisms via BTN2A1. Notably, γδ T cell infiltration is clinically relevant in SCLC, with high levels predictive of improved outcomes with αPD-L1.

articles.title: Ensemble learning of pathology foundation models for precision oncology
articles.abstract: Luo et al. develop ELF, a framework that ensembles five pathology foundation models to generate unified representations from whole-slide images. Trained on nearly 54,000 slides across 20 anatomical sites, ELF outperforms individual foundation models in disease classification, biomarker detection, and prediction of response to chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy.

articles.title: UniCure: A multi-modal model for predicting personalized cancer therapy response
articles.abstract: Chen et al. present UniCure, a multi-modal foundation model that predicts drug-induced transcriptomic responses across diverse cellular contexts. By bridging cancer cell line data with patient-derived models, UniCure enables personalized drug prioritization and patient stratification, with its predicted therapeutic rankings correlating strongly with clinical survival outcomes in real-world cohorts.

articles.title: Myeloid reprogramming generates myeloid-derived activating cells to potentiate radiotherapy and suppress metastasis
articles.abstract: Ji et al. show that radiotherapy induces a TET2-dependent epitranscriptomic program in myeloid cells that promotes immunosuppressive M-MDSC differentiation. TET2 loss preserves caRNA m5C-MBD6 signaling, restores IRF3-IFN-I activation, generates myeloid-derived activating cells, and enhances radiotherapy-induced antitumor immunity.

articles.title: Intratumoral Bacillus cereus orchestrates stem-like lymphoid niches to potentiate immunotherapy response in hepatocellular carcinoma
articles.abstract: Hu et al. integrate spatial multi-omics to identify stem-like lymphoid niches (SLNs) organized by CD70+ ILC2s and Tpex cells that predict PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy responses in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). They reveal that Bacillus cereus-PI-PLC increases SLN abundance and synergizes with PD-L1 blockade, highlighting microbiota-driven enhancement of cancer immunotherapy through SLNs therapeutically in HCC.

articles.title: Proteo-genomics-guided interpretation of somatic mutations in cancer genomes
articles.abstract: Hyeon et al. integrate protein structures with population-scale cancer genomics data to characterize significantly mutated regions in 173 cancer-relevant genes. These regions align with functional domains, three-dimensional structural constraints, and gene-specific biology, providing a framework for classifying mutation patterns in cancer genes and prioritizing sparsely annotated variants for clinical interpretation.

articles.title: A transient MXD4-dependent proliferative pause enables survival of brain micrometastases
articles.abstract: García-Gómez et al. identify a transient state, termed the proliferative pause, that enables the survival of micrometastases during vascular co-option by buffering organ-imposed stress. Targeting vulnerabilities associated with this state suppresses metastatic progression and relapse, revealing opportunities for preventive intervention.

articles.title: Chemotherapy enhances cancer vaccine efficacy and expands stem-like TCF1+CD8+ T cells
articles.abstract: Noblecourt et al. show that chemotherapy acts as an immunological adjuvant by expanding TCF1+CD8+ T cells during vaccine priming, thereby enhancing vaccine-induced anti-tumor immunity. These findings provide a rationale for combining chemotherapy, cancer vaccines, and PD-1 blockade in the clinic.

articles.title: Chemotherapy-free phase 1/2 trial of HRS-4642 plus adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic cancer
articles.abstract: Shi et al. report the first clinical study of the selective KRAS G12D inhibitor HRS-4642 combined with the anti-PD-L1 antibody adebrelimab in heavily pretreated patients with KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic cancer. The chemotherapy-free regimen demonstrates a manageable safety profile and preliminary antitumor activity, supporting its feasibility as a targeted strategy in this molecularly defined subset.

articles.title: TRANSFORM-1 phase 3 study: efficacy and safety of navitoclax plus ruxolitinib in patients with untreated myelofibrosis.
articles.abstract: The phase 3 TRANSFORM-1 study evaluated ruxolitinib (RUX) in combination with navitoclax (NAV) or placebo (PBO) in Janus kinase inhibitor-naïve adults with intermediate-2 or high-risk myelofibrosis and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of ≤2. Patients were randomized 1:1 to NAV (200 mg/d starting dose, or 100 mg escalated to 200 mg/d) or PBO, with RUX dosed per label. The primary end point was ≥35% spleen volume reduction (SVR) at week 24 (SVR35W24). Secondary end points included change from baseline in total symptom score (TSS) at week 24 and SVR35 at any time. A total of 252 patients (NAV+RUX, n = 125; PBO+RUX, n = 127; median follow-up 20.3 months) were randomized; >80% had intermediate-2 risk, and ∼50% had high-molecular risk disease. SVR35W24 was achieved by 63.2% with NAV+RUX vs 31.5% with PBO+RUX (P< .0001). Mean change in TSS at week 24 was not significantly different between NAV+RUX and PBO+RUX (-10.2 vs -11.6; P = .2852). SVR35 at any time was achieved in 76.8% with NAV+RUX vs 44.1% with PBO+RUX (nominal P< .0001). A ≥20% variant allele frequency reduction (exploratory end point) occurred in 58.5% (95% confidence interval [CI], 49.0-67.5) with NAV+RUX and 45.5% (95% CI, 36.4-54.8) with PBO+RUX. NAV+RUX showed higher hematologic toxicity vs PBO+RUX (grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia, 54.0% vs 19.2%; grade 3/4 neutropenia, 40.3% vs 8.8%); diarrhea (any grade, 41.9% vs 16.8%) was also more common. Cytopenias were generally manageable and reversible with dose adjustments. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT04472598.

articles.title: Targeting RAS in pancreatic cancer.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains among the most lethal malignancies, and activating KRAS mutations occur in more than 90% of tumors. Direct RAS targeting has moved from proof of concept to randomized clinical benefit: in previously treated metastatic PDAC, daraxonrasib improved median overall survival, progression-free survival, and objective response rate versus chemotherapy. Mutation-selective G12C and G12D inhibitors, targeted degraders, and first-line RAS(ON) combinations further broaden the landscape. Comprehensive germline and somatic profiling remains essential even with the availability of multi-selective KRAS inhibitors. KRAS alleles differ biologically, drug activity against individual alleles is not yet fully characterized, and eligibility for clinical trials often depends on the specific genotype. In addition, KRAS wild-type tumors may harbor actionable alterations, including gene fusions, amplifications, or mismatch-repair deficiency. This review synthesizes RAS biology, molecular-testing implications, clinical efficacy and toxicity data, and ongoing phase 2 and phase 3 trials. Priority questions include optimal sequencing, management of rash and mucositis, resistance, biomarker development, and integration into first-line and curative-intent therapy.

articles.title: Regional practice differences significantly affect the benefit of post-HCT gilteritinib in FLT3-ITD AML.
articles.abstract: BMT CTN 1506 (MORPHO) was a phase 3 study of post-hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) maintenance with gilteritinib vs placebo for patients with FLT3-ITD-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in first remission. Subgroup analysis indicated a significant benefit of post-HCT gilteritinib for participants in North America but no benefit for those in Europe or Asia. We conducted a post hoc analysis of the data focusing on the time from AML diagnosis to HCT, pre-HCT FLT3 inhibitor use, and FLT3-ITD measurable residual disease (MRD). Participants who underwent transplantation <120 days from AML diagnosis and/or those treated with FLT3 inhibition before HCT were more likely to have improved survival from post-HCT gilteritinib. Pre-HCT MRD levels were higher (P = .001) in participants who underwent transplantation within 120 days from diagnosis and in those treated with an FLT3 inhibitor before HCT and underwent transplantation within 120 days (P = .008). Pre-HCT MRD was dependent on both FLT3 inhibitor use and time to HCT, because participants treated with successive courses of chemotherapy + FLT3 inhibition had successively lower MRD by the time of HCT. Time from AML diagnosis to HCT and pre-HCT FLT3 inhibitor use both appeared to affect MRD levels immediately before HCT, and geographic differences in these 2 practice patterns likely accounted for the observed regional differences in benefit from post-HCT gilteritinib. Increasing the number of courses of treatment before HCT may lower MRD sufficiently to eliminate the need for post-HCT inhibition, but with a presumed risk of some patients experiencing early progression. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as #NCT02997202.

articles.title: EZH2 Inhibition and Myeloid Risk: A Feature of On-Target Biology.
articles.abstract: In March 2026, Ipsen voluntarily withdrew the enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) inhibitor tazemetostat (Tazverik) from all markets and indications following results from the confirmatory phase Ib/III SYMPHONY-1 trial demonstrating hematologic second primary malignancies (SPM) in 5.7% of treated patients, compared with none in the control arm. The most frequently reported SPMs were myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Although this finding may be interpreted as an idiosyncratic liability of a single agent, the biology of EZH2 suggests a broader, target-driven risk. EZH2 functions in a context-dependent manner as both an oncogene and a tumor suppressor. Gain-of-function mutations drive transformation in germinal center B-cell lymphomas, whereas loss-of-function alterations impair hematopoietic stem cell differentiation and are recurrent in myeloid malignancies, including MDS and AML. In selected solid tumor contexts, such as specific subtypes of medulloblastoma, EZH2 loss can likewise promote tumorigenesis. These observations raise concern that chronic pharmacologic inhibition of EZH2 may phenocopy loss-of-function states that initiate myeloid neoplasia. We argue that the withdrawal of tazemetostat exposes a fundamental vulnerability in the development of epigenetic therapies: Target validation has focused on tumor-intrinsic effects while underweighting consequences in normal stem cell compartments. This issue is particularly relevant for ongoing phase III programs in prostate cancer, in which prolonged exposure may amplify latency-dependent risks. We propose changes to preclinical safety assessment, trial design, and pharmacovigilance to mitigate predictable, target-mediated toxicities.

articles.title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology.
articles.abstract: Proton therapy offers a distinct physical advantage over photon radiotherapy through the Bragg peak dose concentration in target with both lower integral dose and finite path length, and sharper penumbra as compared to photons, collectively reducing radiation exposure to surrounding normal tissues and potentially improving the therapeutic ratio. However, this advantage is tempered by uncertainties, including range uncertainty and variable relative biological effectiveness. In this review, the authors summarize contemporary evidence supporting proton therapy across pediatric, central nervous system (CNS), head and neck, thoracic, breast, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and hematologic malignancies, as well as reirradiation. The strength of evidence varies substantially by disease site. Proton therapy is well established in pediatric cancers and selected CNS tumors, where minimizing integral dose and late toxicity is especially important. Randomized trials have demonstrated clinically meaningful benefits in selected settings, including improved disease control and survival with proton craniospinal irradiation for leptomeningeal metastases and reduced toxicity with preserved disease control and survival benefit in oropharyngeal cancer. Conversely, randomized data in localized prostate cancer have not shown improved patient reported outcomes compared with intensity modulated photon therapy. Ongoing phase 3 trials across multiple disease sites are expected to further define the role of protons by clarifying comparative effectiveness, toxicity reduction, and cost-effectiveness relative to advanced photon techniques. Future progress will depend on improved patient selection, robust treatment planning, and emerging technologies including adaptive proton therapy, proton arc therapy, and FLASH radiotherapy.

articles.title: Impact of EBV status and histology on patient outcomes with nivolumab-AVD vs BV-AVD in advanced classic Hodgkin lymphoma (S1826).
articles.abstract: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) positive status as well as nonnodular sclerosis (non-NS) histologic subtypes has demonstrated poorer outcomes compared with EBV- and NS tumors. We report a prespecified subset analysis of patients enrolled in the phase 3 SWOG S1826 trial to evaluate outcomes based on EBV status and histologic subtype in patients treated with N-AVD (nivolumab-AVD) or BV-AVD (brentuximab vedotin-AVD). In the phase 3 SWOG S1826 trial, patients with stage III to IV cHL were randomized to N-AVD or BV-AVD treatment. Of 970 eligible patients, 522 had known EBV status. N-AVD improved 3-year progression-free survival (PFS) in patients who were EBV+ (91% vs 70%; hazard ratio [HR], 0.30; P = .01) and EBV- (90% vs 84%; HR, 0.64; P = .09). Among 664 patients with slides available for histology review, 102 (15.4%) had non-NS histologic subtypes. N-AVD prolonged 3-year PFS in patients with non-NS histologic subtype (86% vs 63%; HR, 0.33; P = .006) and NS histologic subtype (93% vs 86%; HR, 0.53; P = .01). Non-NS histologic subtype was independently associated with inferior outcomes (HR, 2.54; P< .0001) after adjusting for treatment in the entire cohort. However, N-AVD treatment still had favorable PFS within this high-risk group. In addition, patients with EBV+ status or non-NS histologic subtype cHL treated with BV-AVD had significantly worse PFS (HR, 1.97; P = .03 for EBV and HR, 3.08; P< .0001 for histology). N-AVD substantially abrogated the historically poor prognosis associated with EBV+ status and non-NS histologic subtype in advanced-stage cHL. These results support N-AVD as a frontline standard of care, particularly in high-risk biologic subgroups. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03907488.

articles.title: Tumor-Regional Immune Microenvironment: A Critical Factor in the Design of Radiotherapy-Immunotherapy Combination Trials.
articles.abstract: Clinical trials combining radiotherapy (RT) with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) have shown improved outcomes in only a fraction of patients, and optimal strategies for integrating these modalities remain under intense investigation. With a few exceptions, phase III combination trials have yielded disappointing results. This may be due to detrimental effects of RT on the tumor-regional immune microenvironment (TRIME), including tumor-draining lymph nodes (TDLNs) and intratumoral immune aggregates such as tertiary lymphoid structures. TDLNs are crucial for generating tumor-specific T cells, including progenitors of exhausted T cells. Intratumoral immune aggregates are hubs for immune cell interaction participating in induction or reactivation of antitumor immune responses. Understanding the biological role of the TRIME in RT/ICB-induced antitumor immunity is therefore essential for designing RT-immunotherapy combination trials. This review also highlights several potential strategies to optimize RT/ICB combination therapy. One approach involves modifying treatment schedules, for example, delaying RT to TDLNs until after ICB to allow effective immune priming. Another promising strategy is the integration of advanced imaging techniques into RT planning to improve precision and minimize radiation exposure to TDLNs. Applying unconventional RT with lower total dose or to selective areas may help preserve immune aggregates within tumors, potentially enhancing synergy with ICB. Another important approach is the use of dendritic cell agonists to boost the function of the TRIME. These approaches may help unlock the full therapeutic potential of RT/ICB combinations.

articles.title: MRD negativity by PBMCs and ctDNA confirms deep and durable responses after epcoritamab monotherapy in R/R FL.
articles.abstract: In EPCORE NHL-1, the CD3 × CD20 bispecific antibody epcoritamab demonstrated promising efficacy and manageable safety in patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) follicular lymphoma (FL) after ≥2 prior lines of therapy. Using the clonoSEQ assay, we evaluated minimal residual disease (MRD) status using peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and/or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) at prespecified time points and investigated their correlation with clinical outcomes. Epcoritamab induced rapid conversion to MRD negativity, with most MRD-evaluable patients reaching MRD negativity by cycle 3 (C3) day 1 (D1) as measured by either analyte. MRD negativity at C3D1 landmark by either analyte correlated with prolonged progression-free survival (PFS; median not reached), irrespective of radiographic response status. PFS was comparable among patients with overall MRD negativity by PBMCs or ctDNA, regardless of challenging-to-treat disease features. By C3D1 and C5D1 landmarks, patients with complete or partial response, as assessed by positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), who were MRD positive had a shorter PFS compared with those who were MRD negative. In multivariable analyses at week 12 and week 18 PET/CT landmarks, MRD-negative responders by PBMC assessment (week 12) and by both PBMC and ctDNA assessment (week 18) had significantly improved PFS when adjusted for baseline clinical risk factors. These analyses demonstrate that MRD negativity is associated with rapid molecular responses to epcoritamab and prolonged PFS in patients with R/R FL, underscoring the value of MRD analysis to complement conventional response assessment. These findings may aid future clinical trial design or clinical practice in FL. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03625037.

articles.title: Ponatinib-Blinatumomab or Imatinib-Chemotherapy for Adult Ph-Positive ALL.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The outcome of Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-positive ALL) has greatly improved with the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy. METHODS: In this trial, we randomly assigned adult patients with Ph-positive ALL in a 2:1 ratio to receive ponatinib plus blinatumomab (intervention group) or imatinib plus chemotherapy (control group) as frontline treatment. A crossover to the intervention group was allowed for patients with persistence or reappearance of measurable residual disease in the control group. The primary end point was event-free survival. RESULTS: A total of 236 patients underwent randomization: 158 to the intervention group and 78 to the control group. The median age of the patients was 55 years (range, 24 to 82). At a median follow-up of 23.7 months, the estimated 24-month event-free survival was 86% in the intervention group and 67% in the control group (P<0.001). Survival with no measurable residual disease was 68% and 42%, respectively. At the end of induction, a complete hematologic response was observed in 94% of the patients in the intervention group and in 79% of those in the control group. After blinatumomab consolidation, a molecular response was observed in 71% and 49% of the patients, respectively. After crossover to the intervention group, 20 of 31 patients (64%) had a molecular response. Overall survival was 90% in the intervention group and 85% in the control group. The cumulative incidence of relapse was 5% and 13%, respectively. As of this report, only 19% of the patients in the intervention group had undergone hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation after having had a first complete hematologic response. CONCLUSIONS: In this phase 3 trial, a frontline chemotherapy-free targeted and immunotherapeutic approach was superior to the use of imatinib and chemotherapy. (Funded by Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro and others; GIMEMA ALL2820 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04722848.).

articles.title: Oncological impact of adjuvant chemotherapy after rectal cancer excision in the era of FOLFIRINOX-based TNT: A pooled post-hoc analysis of GRECCAR4-PRODIGE23.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The role of adjuvant chemotherapy (AC) after total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) remains controversial, mainly based on colon cancer protocols, with recent validation of the equivalence of the 3- and 6-month CT regimens. The aim of this study is to evaluate the oncological impact of AC in the era of TNT in patients with LARC. METHODS: We conducted a post hoc analysis of ypN+ and ypN0/cN+ subgroups from two French multicentre randomized trials GRECCAR 4(NCT01333709) and PRODIGE 23(NCT01804790). Patients received either long-course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) or TNT with FOLFIRINOX 4-6 cycles followed by CRT.In each subgroup, outcomes of patients who received AC (AC+) were compared with those who did not(AC-).The primary outcome was 3-year Disease-free survival(DFS).Secondary endpoints included 3-year overall survival(OS),distant metastasis and local recurrence free-survival(3y-DMFS and 3y-LRFS). Survivals were adjusted on propensity score. RESULTS: Among 489 patients were eligible, 152 AC- (25ypN+ and 127ypN0/cN+)vs 337 AC+ (119 ypN+ and 218 ypN0/cN+).Baseline tumor characteristics were similar. Median follow-up was 70 months. Overall 3y-DFS was 77% and was significantly improved in AC+ group for ypN+ after CRT (p < 0.001), but not after TNT. For ypN0/cN+, no statistically significant association was observed regarding the 3y-DFS whatever the neoadjuvant treatment,TNT (p = 0.33) or CRT (p = 0.45).Similarly, the AC+ group had a significantly better 3y-OS (p < 0.001), 3y-DMFS (p ≤ 0.001) and 3y-LRFS (p ≤ 0.001) for ypN+ after CRT, but not after TNT. For ypN0/cN+, there was no significant difference between the 2 groups regarding 3y-OS(p = 0.74), 3y-DMFS(p = 0.72) and 3y-LRFS(p = 0.71),whatever the neoadjuvant treatment. CONCLUSIONS: Adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with significantly improved oncological outcomes in ypN+ patients after CRT, whereas no significant association was observed after TNT, irrespective of nodal status. These findings may support de-escalation of adjuvant therapy in the TNT era and inform a more individualised postoperative strategy.

articles.title: Perioperative immunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Outcomes for patients with resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remain suboptimal despite multimodal therapy, with high rates of recurrence and patients suffering from toxicity of treatments. Immune checkpoint inhibitors, which have transformed the management of recurrent and metastatic disease, have been advanced into the perioperative and adjuvant settings. Recent phase III trials mark a turning point: the addition of adjuvant nivolumab improved disease-free survival in pathologic high-risk resected HNSCCs, while perioperative pembrolizumab significantly prolonged event-free survival in resectable locally advanced HNSCCs, supporting a shift toward integrated perioperative immunotherapy strategies. Although the former approach fits into a conventional adjuvant framework, biological insights suggest that neoadjuvant delivery enables effective immune priming extending therapeutic approaches. Together, these advances redefine therapeutic strategies in resectable HNSCC and highlight the potential of perioperative immunotherapy to improve long-term outcomes.

articles.title: FDA Approval Summary: Erdafitinib for FGFR3-Altered Locally Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
articles.abstract: On January 19, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted traditional approval to erdafitinib for patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (la/mUC) with susceptible FGFR3 genetic alterations, as determined by an FDA-approved companion diagnostic test, whose disease has progressed on or after at least one line of prior systemic therapy. Substantial evidence of effectiveness was obtained from BLC3001 (THOR, NCT03390504) Cohort 1, which was an open-label trial in which 266 patients with FGFR3-altered la/mUC were randomized 1:1 to receive erdafitinib (8 mg once daily with potential uptitration to 9 mg) compared with chemotherapy (docetaxel 75 mg/m2 every 3 weeks or vinflunine 320 mg/m2 every 3 weeks) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Statistically significant improvements in OS, progression-free survival, and objective response rate were demonstrated for erdafitinib compared with chemotherapy. The median OS was 12.1 months [95% confidence interval (CI), 10.3-16.4] in the erdafitinib arm and 7.8 months (95% CI, 6.5-11.1) in the chemotherapy arm [hazard ratio (HR), 0.64; 95% CI, 0.47-0.88; P = 0.0050]. Based on BLC3001 Cohort 2 results showing no OS benefit of erdafitinib compared with pembrolizumab (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 0.92-1.51), the approval includes a limitation of use: Erdafitinib is not recommended for the treatment of patients who are eligible for and have not received prior PD-(L)1 inhibitor therapy. This article summarizes the data and the FDA thought process supporting the traditional approval of erdafitinib, including the rationale for not requiring specific types of prior systemic therapy in the indication statement.

articles.title: Longitudinal plasma phosphorylated neurofilament-heavy chain levels in oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy: a prospective multi-institutional exploratory study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Reliable circulating biomarkers for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) remain lacking. Phosphorylated neurofilament-heavy chain (pNF-H) is an axon-oriented biomarker of neuroaxonal injury, but its clinical relevance in oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy has not been established. We evaluated the feasibility and longitudinal behavior of plasma pNF-H in patients receiving oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. METHODS: This prospective multi-institutional exploratory study included patients with unresectable or recurrent colorectal cancer receiving CapeOX plus bevacizumab as part of the NYX study, a randomised trial of ninjin'yoeito (NYT; TJ-108, Tsumura & Co., Tokyo, Japan), a twelve-ingredient Kampo herbal extract, at 9.0 g/day for 24 weeks in the NYT arm. Plasma samples were collected at baseline, at clinically assessed CIPN onset (follow-up 1), and at the time of neuropathy resolution, at cycle 9, or at discontinuation, whichever came first (follow-up 2). Plasma pNF-H concentrations were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. CIPN was assessed using CTCAE version 5.0. RESULTS: Thirty patients with evaluable plasma samples were included. Plasma pNF-H levels showed substantial inter-individual variability without a consistent temporal pattern. Compared with baseline and CIPN onset, plasma pNF-H levels at follow-up 2 were modestly but significantly increased. However, plasma pNF-H levels were not associated with the onset, severity, or persistence of clinically assessed CIPN. CONCLUSIONS: Although longitudinal plasma pNF-H measurement was technically feasible, pNF-H did not function as a clinically meaningful biomarker for oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy. These findings may reflect a pathophysiological mismatch between dorsal root ganglion neuronal cell body injury and the axon-oriented biological specificity of pNF-H.

articles.title: Feasibility and Activity of Concurrent Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy and Radiotherapy in Patients with High-risk Soft-Tissue Sarcoma.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The ISG-STS 1001 was an international, randomized, phase III trial for localized, high-risk, soft-tissue sarcoma comparing neoadjuvant chemotherapy (ChT) with epirubicin and ifosfamide (EI) versus a histology-tailored regimen. The trial also included a cohort of patients not randomized but just registered and treated with EI. In this study, we analyzed the tolerability and activity of concurrent EI and radiotherapy (RT) in the ISG-STS 1001 trial. PATIENTS AND METHODS: EI consisted of epirubicin 120 mg/m2 plus ifosfamide 9 g/m2 per cycle. RT was delivered at a dose of 44 to 50 Gy preoperatively or 60 to 66 Gy postoperatively. ChT dose intensity (DI), grade ≥3 hematologic toxicities, acute RT-related toxicities, postoperative local complications, and radiologic response by RECIST were compared between the group of patients receiving concurrent preoperative ChT and RT (ChT/RT group) and the group receiving preoperative ChT alone (ChT group). RESULTS: Among the 548 patients enrolled in the ISG-STS 1001 trial, 287 were included in the current analysis (146 received preoperative RT). The median ChT DI was >90% in both groups. Hematologic toxicities were comparable between the 2 groups. With regard to postoperative complications, a higher number of wound dehiscence (9% vs. 3.5%, respectively; P = 0.06) and seroma (10.4% vs. 2.8%, respectively; P = 0.01) were observed in the ChT/RT group compared with the ChT group. A statistically significant association between RECIST response and preoperative RT was found (20.3% and 9.8% in the ChT/RT and ChT groups, respectively; P = 0.02). CONCLUSIONS: Concurrent EI and RT is feasible and safe, resulting in an increased proportion of dimensional responses.

articles.title: A phase 1/1b study of the all-oral regimen CC-486 and venetoclax in acute myeloid leukemia.
articles.abstract: Venetoclax with azacitidine is the standard of care for patients with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) who are unfit for intensive induction chemotherapy. CC-486 is the oral formulation of azacitidine that is currently approved for postinduction chemotherapy maintenance in AML. In this single-center, open-label, phase 1/1b study, we investigated CC-486 and venetoclax in patients with relapsed and refractory AML and in those with newly diagnosed disease. In the dose-escalation phase, patients received CC-486 at 1 of 2 cohorts (200 mg by mouth on days 1-14 and 300 mg by mouth on days 1-14). Venetoclax was given at 400 mg/d by mouth for 28 days after an initial intrapatient dose escalation per the standard of care. Using a 3+3 study design for these 2 cohorts, we determined the recommended dose of CC-486 to be 300 mg daily on days 1 to 14. The most common adverse events included nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, and cytopenias. The incidence of grade ≥3 neutropenia or thrombocytopenia was 97% and 66%, respectively. There were no dose-limiting toxicities in either cohort. The expansion phase of the study consisted of 10 additional patients with relapsed and refractory AML and 16 patients with newly diagnosed AML. Responses were seen in all phases of the study, and 6 patients were successfully bridged to hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Correlative analyses including sequencing and metabolomics performed on patient samples suggested that this regimen had a similar effect on leukemia stem cells compared with conventional (IV) azacitidine and venetoclax. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT05287568.

articles.title: A phase 1b/2 study of ceralasertib, a selective inhibitor of ATR, in patients with relapsed or refractory MDS and CMML.
articles.abstract: Pre-mRNA splicing gene mutations in myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) induce R-loops, which trigger ataxia telangiectasis and Rad3-related kinase (ATR). We studied ceralasertib, an orally bioavailable ATR inhibitor, in adults with relapsed or refractory (R/R) MDS or CMML in a phase 1b/2 study 160mg twice daily during 28-day cycles on 2 dosing schedules: days 1 to 14 (14on/14off) or days 1-7 and 15-21 (7on/7off). Response rates and survival were estimated. Forty-four evaluable patients were treated. Grade ≥3 adverse events included thrombocytopenia (n = 13), anemia (n = 12), neutropenia (n = 9), febrile neutropenia (n = 9), pneumonia (n = 6), and hypoxia (n = 5). Thrombocytopenia requiring a platelet transfusion during the first cycle was reduced to 1 of 10 patients on 7on/7off compared with 8/16 patients on 14on/14off among patients with a baseline platelet count >50 × 109/L (P = .087). Overall response rate (ORR) was 29.5% (13/44 patients) and included 1 complete response (CR), 5 marrow CR (2 with hematologic improvement [HI] in neutrophils [HI-N]), and 7 with HI (HI in erythroid/red cells, n = 4; HI-N, n = 2; HI in platelets, n = 1). Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 4.8 months, and overall survival (OS) was 12 months. ORR (P = .72), PFS (P = .9), and OS (P = .65) did not differ between schedules. Splicing factor mutation variant allele frequencies (VAFs) remained stable while RUNX1 mutation VAFs typically increased at progression. Serum inflammatory cytokine levels (TNFRSF8 [CD30], TNF family members) decreased during ceralasertib exposure; this effect was blunted in RUNX1-mutant samples. Ceralasertib 160 mg twice daily on days 1-7 and 15-21 was established as monotherapy dosing. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03770429.

articles.title: HPV Testing Versus Cytology for Cervical Cancer Screening Among Women 50 Years and Older: Evidence From the HPV FOCAL Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: Evidence on the comparative effectiveness of HPV testing versus cytology specifically in women aged ≥ 50 years who are approaching screening cessation remains limited. This analysis included 6471 women aged ≥ 50 at baseline screening in the HPV FOCAL randomized clinical trial. Women were randomly allocated to receive cytology (Control Group, n = 3248, 50.19%) or HPV testing (Intervention Group, n = 3223, 49.81%) at baseline, with co-testing at 48-month exit. We calculated incidence rates and risk ratios for CIN2+ detection over follow-up and compared missed lesions at exit by screening method. At the 48-month exit, CIN2+ detection was lower among HPV baseline-negative women than among those in the cytology group (1.61/1000 [95% CI, 0.52-3.76] vs. 3.15/1000 [95% CI, 1.51-5.78]; risk ratio, 0.51 [95% CI, 0.11-0.91]), reflecting higher baseline detection with HPV testing and fewer prevalent lesions at exit. Even with cytology re-screening at 2 years, 50% of CIN2+ cases were missed compared to 30% with HPV testing. After adjusting for age, education, smoking status, and lifetime sexual partners, the hazard ratio for CIN2+ comparing HPV to cytology was 0.44 (95% CI, 0.22-0.88). Among women aged ≥ 50 years, HPV primary screening was more effective than cytology at detecting CIN2+ lesions and was associated with a continued lower subsequent risk following a negative HPV test, supporting its use in cervical cancer screening programs in this age cohort.

articles.title: Risk-Benefit of Phase 2 Monotherapy Trials in Adult Solid Cancers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Phase 2 (and phase 1 dose expansion, which we label phase 2 for the purposes of this study) cancer trials are the first direct tests of a new drug's efficacy. Because efficacy evidence is lacking, the therapeutic status of drug administration during ethical review is uncertain. We compared the efficacy and safety of cancer monotherapies in phase 2 with phase 3, where clinical equipoise underwrites a therapeutic status for drug administration. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched Clinicaltrials.gov for phase 2 and 3 investigational monotherapy drug trials in six solid malignancies, with primary completion dates 2015-2020, inclusive. Two independent reviewers completed data extraction. Effects were estimated using an inverse-variance weighted random-effects model meta-analysis of proportions using the R package meta. We analyzed 130 phase 2 and 52 phase 3 trial arms, enrolling 6665 and 18,694 patients. The pooled objective response rate was 7% (95% CI 5%-11%) in phase 2 versus 24% in phase 3 (95% CI 17%-31%; p < 0.0001). The median PFS and OS were shorter in phase 2 compared to phase 3 (3.23 vs. 5.43 months, p < 0.0001; 9.46 vs. 14.44 months, p = 0.0001). The pooled rate of drug-related grade 3-4 adverse events was 30% (95% CI 23%-37%) in phase 2 and 25% (95% CI 19%-32%) in phase 3. Monotherapies delivered in phase 2 cancer trials present diminished risk-benefit compared with phase 3 and align with historic estimates for phase 1. Though there may be exceptions, risks for drug administration in phase 2 should generally be justified by appeals to research rather than therapeutic value.

articles.title: Stereotactic body radiotherapy versus conventional external beam radiotherapy for bone metastases: a meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) and conventional external beam radiotherapy (cEBRT) are widely used treatment options for the management of painful bone metastases. Randomized phase III trials have provided direct comparative evidence for SBRT and cEBRT; however, their results vary according to treatment regimen and clinical endpoint, supporting a broader quantitative synthesis of pain response, local control, retreatment, and safety outcomes. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar from database inception through January 2026. Comparative clinical studies evaluating SBRT versus cEBRT for bone metastases were included. Outcomes assessed encompassed pain-related measures (change in Visual Analog Scale scores at 3 and 6 months; complete, partial, stable, and progressive pain response), opioid consumption at 3 and 6 months, radiologic local progression or treatment failure at 8 months, re-irradiation at 12 months, skeletal-related events (vertebral and non-vertebral compression fractures), spinal cord compression, treatment-related toxicity, and overall survival at 1 year. Pooled analyses were performed using random-effects models. Early pain reduction at 3 months, partial and stable pain response, and opioid consumption at 3 and 6 months were comparable between SBRT and cEBRT (all p > 0.05). However, SBRT demonstrated superior mid-term outcomes, with a significantly higher complete pain response at 6 months (RR = 1.43; p = 0.001) and a significantly lower rate of progressive pain response at 6 months (RR = 0.61; p = 0.03). SBRT was also associated with markedly improved local disease control, reflected by lower rates of radiologic local progression or treatment failure at 8 months (RR = 0.36; p < 0.001) and a substantially reduced need for re-irradiation at 12 months (RR = 0.13; p < 0.001). Rates of vertebral and non-vertebral compression fractures, spinal cord compression, treatment-related toxicity, and overall survival at 1 year did not differ significantly between treatment modalities. This meta-analysis demonstrates that both SBRT and cEBRT are safe and effective treatment options for patients with painful bone metastases. While early pain palliation and safety outcomes are comparable, SBRT provides superior durability of pain control, reduced pain progression, improved local tumor control, and a markedly lower need for re-irradiation. SBRT may be particularly advantageous for patients with longer expected survival, oligometastatic disease, or lesions at higher risk of progression, whereas cEBRT remains an effective and accessible option for rapid symptom palliation in patients with limited prognosis.

articles.title: AI-Based Pathology Classifier Predicts Sensitivity to Enzalutamide in Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: A Biomarker Analysis of the ENZAMET Trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The ENZAMET trial established that enzalutamide added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) improves overall survival (OS) in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC), but treatment response is heterogeneous. We tested whether the artificial intelligence pathology image classifier (APIC), previously developed and locked in CHAARTED, predicts OS benefit from enzalutamide in ENZAMET. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: This biomarker study applied APIC to digitized hematoxylin and eosin specimens from ENZAMET [Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group (ANZUP) 1304, NCT02446405]. ENZAMET randomized participants with mHSPC to ADT plus enzalutamide or nonsteroidal antiandrogen (NSAA), with early concurrent docetaxel permitted. APIC was applied without modification or retraining. The prespecified primary analysis evaluated the treatment-by-APIC interaction for OS using Cox models adjusted for standard clinical factors. Prespecified sensitivity analysis excluded participants receiving early concurrent docetaxel. RESULTS: Among 1,125 participants, 492 with digitized tissue (median follow-up, 68.8 months) were eligible. APIC classified 316 (64%) as APIC negative and 176 (36%) as APIC positive. APIC significantly modified enzalutamide benefit (interaction P = 0.014). APIC-negative disease showed improved survival with enzalutamide versus NSAA [HR, 0.50; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.35-0.73; 60-month OS, 76.5% vs. 58.3%], whereas APIC-positive disease showed limited evidence of benefit (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.67-1.62; 60-month OS, 55.6% vs. 58.8%). In low-volume disease, enzalutamide improved survival in APIC-negative (HR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.16-0.62) but not APIC-positive disease (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.53-2.06; interaction P = 0.015). For non-docetaxel-treated participants, enzalutamide benefit was greater in APIC-negative (HR, 0.40; 60-month OS 82% vs. 61.0%) than in APIC-positive participants (HR, 0.79; 60-month OS, 62.8% vs. 57.6%). CONCLUSIONS: The presence of APIC-negative disease identified participants with a major improvement in OS with the addition of enzalutamide to ADT compared with the addition of NSAA.
