articles.title: Navigating the landscape of targeted therapies for renal cell carcinoma in the era of precision medicine (Review).
articles.abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a biologically heterogeneous malignancy characterized by dysregulation of angiogenic signaling, immune evasion and epigenetic remodeling. Advances in molecular profiling have redefined RCC as a pathway‑driven disease, enabling the development of targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) that have notably improved clinical outcomes. The present review evaluated current evidence on the molecular basis and therapeutic landscape of RCC, with emphasis on von Hippel‑Lindau‑hypoxia‑inducible factor signaling, chromatin remodeling alterations and immune regulatory pathways. The present review summarizes pivotal phase III clinical trials evaluating VEGF‑targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors and combination regimens, including nivolumab plus ipilimumab, pembrolizumab + axitinib and lenvatinib + pembrolizumab. Emerging biomarkers, including International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium risk stratification, programmed death‑ligand 1 expression and chromatin remodeling gene alterations (polybromo 1/BRG1‑associated factor 180, BRCA1‑associated protein 1 and SET domain containing 2), are discussed in the context of their clinical utility and limitations. Despite marked progress, durable predictive biomarkers and optimal treatment sequencing strategies remain unresolved. Resistance to therapy emerges through adaptive angiogenic signaling, immune escape and metabolic reprogramming, underscoring the need for integrated multi‑omics approaches and rational combination strategies. By integrating molecular biology with clinical trial evidence, the present review provides a structured framework for understanding therapeutic decision‑making in RCC and highlights future directions toward biomarker‑guided precision oncology.

articles.title: Neoadjuvant and Perioperative Immunotherapy for Resectable Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Current Evidence, Endpoints, and Clinical Integration.
articles.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are being investigated across curative-intent treatment pathways for resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Randomized studies show that programmed cell death-1 blockade can increase pathological complete response (pCR) when added to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, while immunochemoradiotherapy can produce high pathological response rates. This structured narrative review summarizes current evidence for neoadjuvant and perioperative immunotherapy in ESCC within the context of established chemotherapy and chemoradiotherapy backbones. Particular attention is given to randomized ICI trials, the role of radiotherapy, interpretation of pathological and survival endpoints, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), postoperative therapy, perioperative safety, clinical response assessment, and regional applicability. pCR is a useful early activity endpoint and may carry prognostic information within individual regimens, but definitions and pathological assessment vary and trial-level surrogacy for overall survival has not been established. Longitudinal ctDNA is promising as a complementary measure of molecular residual disease but remains investigational for treatment adaptation. When radiotherapy is combined with ICI, established thoracic organ-at-risk constraints and careful monitoring for overlapping pulmonary and esophageal toxicity remain important because ICI-specific normal-tissue constraints have not been validated. Clinical complete response assessment also requires multimodal evaluation; post-treatment inflammatory changes can limit CT and PET-CT specificity. Overall, current data support continued phase III evaluation of ICI-containing strategies with mature event-free and overall survival endpoints and with comparators appropriate to regional treatment standards.

articles.title: Novel antibody-based regimens for large B-cell lymphoma: latest updates from the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting.
articles.abstract: Large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) encompasses a biologically and clinically heterogeneous group of aggressive B-cell lymphomas, and outcomes remain poor in high-risk and relapsed/refractory settings. Beyond conventional anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies, the Fc-modified anti-CD19 antibody tafasitamab, the CD79b-directed antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin, and CD20×CD3 bispecific antibodies are expanding treatment options across disease stages and patient populations. At the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, the phase 3 frontMIND trial provided randomized evidence for tafasitamab plus lenalidomide and R-CHOP in newly diagnosed high-risk disease, while OLYMPIA-3 further explored CD20×CD3 bispecific antibody intensification in the same setting. In older or treatment-unfit patients, early-phase nonrandomized studies of epcoritamab plus R-mini-CVP and mosunetuzumab monotherapy suggested the feasibility of chemotherapy-attenuated and chemotherapy-free approaches. In relapsed/refractory LBCL, SUNMO established a progression-free survival advantage for mosunetuzumab plus polatuzumab vedotin in autologous stem-cell transplantation (ASCT)-ineligible disease, whereas EPCORE NHL-2 supported epcoritamab-based salvage therapy in transplant-eligible patients. Collectively, these findings broaden the role of antibody-based regimens from frontline intensification and reduced-intensity treatment to nontransplant and transplant-directed salvage. Longer follow-up and randomized comparisons are needed to establish response durability, refine patient selection, and define optimal treatment sequencing.

articles.title: Opioid-free versus opioid-based anesthesia for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy: a single-center randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia is standard in urological surgery, and there is additional interest in eliminating intraoperative opioids in prostate cancer surgery. Randomized evidence for opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) in robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) is lacking. In this single-center randomized controlled trial, adult men undergoing RARP were allocated 1:1 to OFA (dexmedetomidine plus ketamine, no intraoperative opioids) or a remifentanil-based technique. Both groups received identical multimodal premedication, a bilateral quadratus lumborum block, sevoflurane maintenance and identical oxycodone patient-controlled analgesia (PCA). The primary outcome was cumulative PCA oxycodone consumption over the first 24 postoperative hours. Prespecified secondary outcomes were pain (NRS), postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), the demanded-to-delivered PCA bolus ratio, and perioperative changes in serum creatinine and white-cell count. A total of 149 patients were analyzed (OFA n=75, opioid-based n=74). Cumulative 24-h oxycodone consumption was lower with OFA (median 12.0 mg [interquartile range, IQR 6.0-22.0] vs 19.0 mg [10.5-34.0]; p=0.001), with a Hodges-Lehmann location-shift estimate of -6.0 mg (95% confidence interval, CI -10.0 to -2.0). Pain scores did not differ at any time point, and PONV was infrequent, with no significant between-group difference. Intraoperative hemodynamic adverse events (bradycardia, hypotension), perioperative white-cell count and serum creatinine did not differ between groups. In RARP delivered on a standardized multimodal and regional analgesic background, OFA reduced postoperative opioid consumption compared with a remifentanil-based technique, without a detectable difference in pain scores and with a similar safety profile.Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06380244, registered 23 April 2024.

articles.title: Multimodal assessment of exceptional responders refines subtyping-directed precision treatment in HR+/HER2- breast cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUNDWe previously defined 4 hormone receptor+/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2- (HR+/HER2-) subtypes: SNF1 canonical luminal, SNF2 immunogenic, SNF3 proliferative, and SNF4 RTK driven. The FASCINATE-N proof-of-concept trial demonstrated that subtyping-directed precision treatment improves pathologic complete response in locally advanced HR+/HER2- breast cancer, yet efficacy remains suboptimal.METHODSWe integrated transcriptomic, genomic, digital pathology, and clinical data from this trial (n = 230) and focused on exceptional responders to explore opportunities for refining treatment strategies.RESULTSIn SNF1, we uncovered that perineural invasion diminished endocrine therapy efficacy, suggesting the potential benefit of incorporating perineural blockade. Digital pathology and spatial transcriptomics identified that the spatial architecture of the tumor-stromal-immune interface influenced apatinib efficacy in SNF4, highlighting the importance of interfering with the tumor microenvironment. In the SNF3 group, exceptionally well responders exhibited multiple mutations in DNA repair genes and cell cycle activation, correlating with the efficacy of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase and CDK4/6 inhibitors. Additionally, we illustrated that lymphatic vessel infiltration was linked to improved immunotherapy outcomes in HR+/HER2- SNF2 tumors.CONCLUSIONOverall, our study emphasizes the importance of multimodal assessments in optimizing precision treatments for HR+/HER2- breast cancer.FUNDINGNational Natural Science Foundation of China, grant numbers U25C2032, 82441028, and 82573645; The Shanghai Key Laboratory of Breast Cancer, grant number 12DZ2260100; The Human Phenome Data Center of Fudan University.TRIAL REGISTRATIONClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05582499.

articles.title: 70-gene signature MammaPrint for early-stage HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer: Outcome in the MINDACT trial for key clinical-pathological high-risk subgroups.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adjuvant chemotherapy (ACT) can be safely omitted in patients above 50 years of age with stage I-II hormone receptor positive (HR+) HER2-negative (HER2-) breast cancer and a low-risk 70-gene signature (MammaPrint®). However, the contribution of the 70-gene signature in high-risk subgroups by nodal involvement, grade 3 or larger tumors, has not been reported, which may complicate clinical decision making for these patients. PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients above 50 years enrolled in the MINDACT trial with primary stage I-II HR + HER2- breast cancer and a clinical high/genomic low-risk were selected for this exploratory analysis. In the MINDACT trial, these patients were randomized at enrollment based on their risk assessment method for the decision to receive ACT or not. Eight-year distant metastasis free survival (DMFS) was the primary endpoint. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 8.7 years. Of the 868 clinical high/genomic low-risk MINDACT patients, 490 (56.5%) patients had tumors larger than 2 cm, 232 (26.7%) had grade 3 tumors and 406 (46.8%) had 1-3 involved lymph nodes. 8-year DMFS in the no ACT group was 87.9% (95%CI: 82.9-91.6%) in patients with tumors larger than 2 cm; 91.3% (95%CI: 84.0-95.4%) with grade 3 tumors and 89.6% (95%CI: 84.2-93.3%) with nodal involvement. Absolute 8-year DMFS benefit for ACT versus no ACT was 1.2%; -2.2% and 0.7% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory subgroup analysis of the MINDACT trial confirms the prognostic performance of the 70-gene signature in patients with high-risk features such as larger tumors, grade 3 tumors and 1-3 involved lymph nodes.
